utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we will go through to 4.00 as you requested and then we will take a 20 minute break before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to say that I have noticed three errors in my written final brief, which I wish to correct now. Although I do not think they are important. One is in the table of contents, under number 8, where witness VG81 is incorrectly marked VGD81. And on page 41, instead of Pionirska Street, in the afternoon, it should read, in the evening hours. And another error I noticed is on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Whereabouts on page 41? In the heading? I see. In the heading? It should be evening hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on page 108, in the last line, it says, "VG133." It should read VG13. I apologise for these errors. Your Honour, I shall continue my closing arguments, from the point where I explained whether Mitar Vasiljevic, based on the submissions of the Prosecution, really was or was not a member of Milan Lukic's group. One of the arguments of the Prosecution, to support this claim, was the fact that Mitar Vasiljevic said certain things in his testimony. And I would like to take a few minutes to talk about this in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We will go into private session. How long do you think you will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: A few minutes only, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are now back in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our view, the Defence has provided evidence to show where Mitar Vasiljevic spent the time from the 19th or the 20th of May when the Uzice Corps withdrew from Visegrad, to the 14th of June, 1992. Until the end of May, he was in Prelovo as a mobilised member of the Territorial Defence, where he worked in the kitchen, and this was borne out by the testimony of a number of witnesses whom I have mentioned in the final brief, so I will not repeat what they said now. After he left Prelovo in early June, Mitar Vasiljevic spent a few days in Uzamnica because of the incident in the headquarters when he gave back his weapons and refused to go back to Prelovo. After these few days, in the view of the Defence, this was around the 3rd of June, he was released from prison, and the reason for this seems to have been that he wanted to attend the funeral of his cousin. Evidently, however, no other measures were pronounced against him for what he had done and this was probably due to his behaviour and the danger that he might cause an incident in Prelovo, so that as far as his obligation toward the Territorial Defence went, he was relieved of his duty and his weapons, and was instead charged with another duty, which was almost humiliating and this was to look after the cleanliness of the town. It's hard to imagine that a member of a group such as Milan Lukic's unit, which consisted of young, well-equipped, well-armed men who were always on the move, as is evident from the evidence produced in this case, to have in their ranks someone like Mitar Vasiljevic and for the reasons I have put forward, this was also physically impossible. In our view, the evidence produced in this case shows that there is no evidence to show that he actually belonged to Milan Lukic's paramilitary unit. Mr. Groome in his closing arguments did say that if he did not belong to the group formally, he could have belonged to it informally. It is difficult to imagine what kind of membership we are talking about here, informal and formal membership of the group, and whether this informal membership in the group would also imply an ad hoc membership in a specific moment, at a specific time, which cannot be accepted, nor can it be used as a proof for something that is quite crucial in this case, namely the possible participation in common design and perpetration of criminal acts. Therefore, we believe, Your Honours, that neither formal nor Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. informal membership can be ascribed to Mitar Vasiljevic, and it is our submission that the situations which were discussed here in this case, namely when he was in the company of Milan Lukic, were sufficiently explained, and as such cannot be used as evidence to support this fact, to prove this fact. Let me now try to analyse some of the facts which concern the events of the 14th of June, 1992. After that, and after I assess a number of other facts and evidence about this incident, I should like to turn to the so-called Drina River incident and give you my interpretation of that incident. It is not disputed that Mitar Vasiljevic was present at this incident. However, what we do dispute is his participation in the incident. I will try not to repeat what is already stated in the final brief of the Defence and concentrate on certain crucial points which I believe are significant for the purposes of assessing the testimony of witnesses who testify about the events of the 14th of June, 1992. First of all, we are faced with a very important issue from the perspective of the Defence, which is whether Mitar Vasiljevic was at any point in time on this day in the centre of the town before the new hotel in Visegrad, in front of the new hotel in Visegrad, where the group from Koritnik had gathered, the group which was late for the bus. We believe, Your Honours, this to be very important also in view of the fact that the indictment charges the accused Vasiljevic with sending this group from Koritnik to Pionirska Street and with placing them in the Memic house. Witnesses of the events which occurred in front of the hotel in Visegrad are six in total, and they were also witnesses as to the events which happened later on that day, because all six of them from -- were part of this group that had come from Koritnik. The Chamber and other participants in these proceedings know who these witnesses are and I should like to move directly to the assessment of the Defence of their testimony regarding these particular events. As for these six witnesses, three testified that they had not seen Mitar Vasiljevic in front of the Visegrad Hotel. They also testified that he had not gone with them. They testified that he -- they did not testify that he had gone with them to Pionirska Street. I'm referring to witnesses VG13, 18, and 84. Let me first dwell on the testimony of these three witnesses, who spoke about having seen Mitar Vasiljevic, because I think that from what they testified before the Court, and in view of their prior statements as to the same events, it follows quite clearly that they were not in a position to see Mitar Vasiljevic in front of the hotel on that day, that they could not have seen him. Out of these three witnesses, two are sisters and they did not part at any point in time on that day, as they testified. However nevertheless, they provided two very different testimonies about this event. One of them, VG78, testified that she had seen Mitar Vasiljevic immediately together with other individuals in front of the hotel. Furthermore, that he had a rifle slung on his shoulder, a fact which was not seen by any of the witnesses later that day, including in Pionirska Street. Quite the contrary. We heard testimony that he did not have a rifle in Pionirska Street. However, this person stated that an individual whom she identified as Mitar Vasiljevic followed them to Pionirska Street together with two or three other armed individuals. Your Honour, it is the opinion of the Defence that this witness, as well as her sister, VG101, at that time did not actually know Mitar Vasiljevic at all, and that if they gave a description of an individual in front of the hotel in this way, we submit, Your Honours, that they must have referred to another individual, because the sister of this witness, VG101, testified that the individual whom she had identified as Mitar Vasiljevic had arrived by car. She could not remember the car, she could not provide any further explanation. However, she was sure that he had arrived in a car, and that he had also left later on in a car, which is not credible in view of the fact that Mitar Vasiljevic never owned a car or a driver's licence for that matter, nor did he ever drive any car, and except for this witness, no one ever saw him in such a situation. This witness described the individual in question as wearing a big chain and a cross. Now, this is something that no one ever saw on Mitar, neither on that day nor later on the same day, and we believe that it is evident that unless this witness has invented such an individual, that this must have been someone else and not Mitar Vasiljevic. It is interesting to point out the fact that this witness stated that no one had followed them to Pionirska Street, which is different from the testimony of her sister, who was always with her, and who stated that they had been escorted by two or three individuals, including Mitar Vasiljevic, or the individuals whom she identified as being Mitar Vasiljevic. What we believe to be quite significant and rather telling, as regards the testimony of VG78, is the fact, Your Honours, that both before the Chamber during the cross-examination, when confronted with her statement given to the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, she admitted that she had given a statement to that effect. She confirmed that it was indeed her statement, and the statement reads as follows in this respect: "There was a certain Mitar near the hotel at the time, a Mitar from Pozdercici whose surname I don't know. He was wearing civilian clothes and a traditional Serb hat on his head, whereas others were wearing camouflage uniforms." The witness gave this statement in 1995, some three years after the events, and it is quite clear that if she was indeed speaking about this Mitar, because Mitar Vasiljevic, as we know, is not from Pozdercici, nor did he ever wear sajkaca, the traditional Serbian hat, she was probably thinking of another individual whom she didn't know by name or surname. In view of that, it is quite strange that a year ago, and now, before the Court, that she should know the surname of the individual whom she had not known before, and that she knew a number of other things about him. The third witness who claimed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, everything you've told us about the two twin sisters are in your final brief. You haven't given us any new information about it. Now, please do proceed upon the basis that we have read your final submission. What we want you to do is to elaborate something if it can be elaborated, but you've spent now 20 minutes telling us what's on one page of a document of 120 something pages long. Now, we will be here for weeks if we go at this rate. We have read your submissions, they are very helpful. There are a few questions we will be asking you about them later but we would like you to deal with other material now, not what we've already read.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] It is quite possible, I'm afraid, that I am repeating myself, but I deemed this to be very important. Let me finish with just a few words about this third witness who apparently had seen this person talking to Lipovac for about ten minutes, though it is quite evident that the individual in question had never reached Visegrad, and that he was at the head of the column for Pionirska Street. As for the three persons who did not see Mitar Vasiljevic, the most important in my opinion is the fact that VG13 was able to fully recognise the person who was in uniform and to whom she had spoken and who had issued them some instructions. She told us that this was Brane Tesevic, a waiter from Visegrad. There is no reason not to believe this witness, and Witness VG18, who claimed that Mitar Vasiljevic was not in front of the hotel. In particular, because of the fact that VG13 is a witness who severely charged Mitar Vasiljevic for his participation in what happened later that evening. So she surely would not have said that the individual in question was Brane Tesevic, the person who was in front of the hotel, if that had been Mitar Vasiljevic. Mitar Vasiljevic, furthermore, could not have been in front of the hotel at the time, and I think that this is a fact which could have been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. easily established from the testimony of Prosecution witness VG87, who almost one hour before the Koritnik group reached the Memic house had seen Mitar Vasiljevic walking along that street. He described him the way he saw him, and he also told us what he had in his hand. I do not wish to go into details, because they are contained in my brief. However, let me just point out that it is the testimony of this witness that indicates that Mitar Vasiljevic was not in front of the Visegrad Hotel and that the Koritnik group could have been seen by him only at the same time as it had been seen by VG87, that is at the moment they reached the house belonging to the Memic family, when, according to this witness, they actually entered the house so they were no longer visible to him. VG87 clearly stated that at that moment, Mitar Vasiljevic was in the street in front of his house, but he also stated that he didn't see when he actually went towards this house. But that, however, is not in dispute. It is also not in dispute that at one point in time during that afternoon, Mitar Vasiljevic did find himself in the company of (redacted) (redacted), who was in the Koritnik group and who arrived in Pionirska Street with them. It is not in dispute that they talked, and I believe it is not in dispute that they had a drink together, that they drank brandy, as they had done on numerous previous occasions, because the witnesses knew them both in this context. What is in dispute here is what was actually said in their conversation, and whether Mitar Vasiljevic also talked to other persons and especially whether he made any suggestions or gave them any instructions as to where and how they should go. These facts have been interpreted very differently by all the witnesses who testified here about this event and the six witnesses I mentioned as witnesses to the beginning of the event in front of the Visegrad Hotel. I will not repeat their testimonies, even briefly, because I have summarised them in my final brief, but I will point out certain details which I consider to be important, although most of these witnesses mention a certificate given to (redacted) by Mitar Vasiljevic, they speak quite differently about the circumstances, about the way in which the certificate came to be issued, how, in what manner, and what the certificate actually contained. As regards the certificate, Mitar Vasiljevic stated here that he had tried to remember it but that he was really unable to remember that he gave anything in writing to (redacted), although he allowed for the possibility that perhaps he had done something of the sort, although he couldn't remember it. The question is: Would Mitar Vasiljevic be able to remember anything about this event, had not (redacted), whom he knew well, and whom he remembered, who helped him to remember the events in Pionirska Street. However, not only has time eroded his memory, because Mitar Vasiljevic probably never thought that he would be called upon to remember these details and that after so many years had passed, this would be very important for him personally. Also, I believe that at that moment, he really had been drinking and, of course, after the passage of so much time, this cannot be established. We cannot know whether he was only tipsy or whether he was drunk, whether he was more or less inebriated, but he evidently was under the influence of alcohol and as VG87 explained, he was walking up and down the street, holding a bottle in one hand, and this was certainly the bottle from which he had started drinking even before he met (redacted). And this witness evaluates his behaviour differently now, like all the witnesses who experienced this tragedy in Pionirska Street and who, in my view, have been trying to identify and establish persons who, apart from the direct perpetrators, may have played a role. This is what this witness, as well as some other witnesses, is trying, in view of the behaviour of Mitar Vasiljevic on that afternoon, to understand. They are trying to establish that his behaviour could have had some connection with what happened to them later in the course of that evening. In my view, the behaviour of Mitar Vasiljevic on that occasion really has nothing to do with what happened to those people on that evening, with what Milan Lukic and the others did to them. Not only because Mitar Vasiljevic was not a member of this group, and not only because he went directly from that spot to the next village or hamlet to get a horse, which he mounted and then had an accident where he fell off the horse in the town, after which he was taken first to the out-patients clinic and then to the hospital, but because, in my view, Mitar Vasiljevic's behaviour that afternoon, which was not, so to speak, normal, could have resulted only from the fact that he was under the influence of alcohol and this was the reason he behaved in the way described by Witness VG87, who saw him walking up and down the street, saying -- uttering disconnected sentences. He also saw him at a certain point in time barefoot, and if this really happened and it was a cloudy, windy, rainy day, it really was not normal behaviour or the behaviour of a sober person. This could only have meant that this was a man who was under the influence of alcohol and it explains the fact that he can not remember his entire conversation with (redacted) and what many witnesses are saying, that is, that he actually wrote something in his own hand. If we accept that he really did write something at (redacted) (redacted) request or on his own initiative, and that he then handed this to the other man, and if we assume that the content was what only one witness in my view claims to have read, I think the witness is VG13, and according to that witness, what was written on that piece of paper was -- I had read from the transcript in English: "Nobody is going to harm you." [Interpretation] Signed with Mitar Vasiljevic's first and last name. This is what VG13 said in court, although it's telling that she never said this before to the OTP investigator, even though she made her statement three or four years prior to her testimony. In my view, these witnesses obviously have a common purpose, which is to lay the blame at the door of Mitar Vasiljevic for aiding and abetting in what happened to them that night. I am not sure that this whole story involving the certificate is not a total fabrication, because I truly cannot see the importance of a certificate containing this sort of message, written by a man who -- whom they knew either through hearsay or in other ways was a waiter, that he was an alcoholic, who had no position, although I shall go back to this, some witnesses say that he was connected to the Red Cross, but even were this so, what sort of personal guarantee given by a man like that, written by hand and handed over in this manner, could be useful while in the view of the OTP this is a crucial piece of evidence, I think that even the word "intelligent move" was used, intended to deceive these people or to trick them, and in my view, this is not tenable, even had a certificate been written down in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, we will take a 20-minute break now but I've been adding up sometimes. You have had about an hour and a quarter now. We have to finish this afternoon or this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, we will finish, Your Honour, I am sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let's hope, then, that we will be speeding up a little bit through the evidence. We do have most of that already in the final brief that you filed. We will adjourn now until 4.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to speed up a little bit. I'm not going to mention things that have been explained in detail in my brief. However, as for the event which I haven't finished yet, I should like to mention just a few additional things. Apart from what I have said regarding the certificate and its value, if it indeed existed, there is one more fact that needs to be mentioned, that is whether Mitar Vasiljevic was in the position to give such information to this group, that is to give the information about the group to Milan Lukic and his soldiers, as some of these witnesses Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. suspected. This also being the Prosecution case. First of all, their presence in the centre of Visegrad around noon, in front of the hotel. They were seen by a number of people there, including soldiers and police officers, as they themselves testified, and also some individuals who were obviously members of the paramilitary forces. All those who were in the vicinity of the Visegrad Hotel apparently knew that they were going to the Mahala neighbourhood, to Pionirska Street. That group of people could also be easily seen in the very centre of the town, as it was moving in the direction of Pionirska Street. Although it has been alleged here that the area in question was far from the centre of the town, one must mention the fact that Memic's houses are only about 100 metres away from the main road leading from Visegrad towards Uzice, in the area where the petrol station is located, the petrol station which was mentioned by VG77. So their transfer to Pionirska Street could by no means constitute a secret for anyone. On the other hand, the insistence that they should be only in one house has nothing to do with what actually happened that evening. In this regard, let me remind you that the perpetrators of the crime took people not only from the Memics' house to the Omeragic house, but also from the house of VG87, that is his wife and four other persons, which had nothing to do with the Koritnik group. On the other hand, one must not lose sight of the fact that these people reached the Memic house on their own and stayed there because that was the only solution for them at the time. Any instruction or any insistence on the part of anyone, including Mitar Vasiljevic, really had no significance whatsoever, if indeed such an instruction existed. Furthermore, this group of people was at no point in time guarded by anyone, and it is true that they could have, if they wanted or dared, in view of the fact that they were likely to encounter various groups of individuals on their way, gone to some other part of the town. It is obvious, however, that the group wanted to stay together, because they believed that the following morning, they would take the first bus and leave the town, having missed the bus on that day. On the other hand, never, before that day, on the 14th of June, something of this sort had happened in the town of Visegrad. Never did such a large group, including women, children and elderly, never was such a large group exposed or been killed or murdered in this way. So I think that it is not likely that these people feared that. They may have feared the possibility of being robbed, because regrettably, that had already been a common occurrence. Moreover, without having -- without having any witnesses testifying at this Court, people who arrived on that evening, or rather on that afternoon, about this particular fact, it is impossible, it is unacceptable for this certificate to be invoked at all. So it is either that this certificate never really existed or they themselves were aware that such a piece of paper could not help them in cases of such groups, that is groups of paramilitaries. It is true that a witness, a lady witness, mentioned that there was talk about the possibility of showing the certificate to the police, if necessary, which is quite strange, that the police should need a paper of this kind, in particular a certificate issued by Mitar Vasiljevic. I should now like to conclude with this event, which was described in my brief in detail, by saying that it is the position of the Defence that whatever Mitar Vasiljevic may have said or written at that moment, given the situation he was in, cannot be interpreted as any kind of intention to retain these people together so that they can be robbed or killed. Furthermore, he had nothing to do with what later happened to them, although some of them still do not believe this and, in my view, that is the only reason why they wanted to testify that they had seen him, whereas that simply could not have been the case. As regards the other event which took place on that afternoon, that is the arrival of the group of paramilitaries, the robbery and the rape of two women, even here, during the testimony of some of the witnesses, actually in the case of only two witnesses, the mother and the son, VG13 and VG38, only they make mention of the fact that they had seen or heard Mitar Vasiljevic somewhere in the vicinity of the house at the time. I do not want to dwell too long on this issue because the Prosecution has not charged Mitar Vasiljevic with being present amongst the group which arrived in the house on that afternoon, at least this is what we can conclude from count 18. However, the event which followed on that evening is in dispute because Mitar Vasiljevic has been charged with being one of the people who transferred the group of people from the first house to the Omeragic house, and also with being one of the participants in the killing of these people. I will devote sometime to the alibi of the accused, that is the fact that he was not, nor could he be, in Pionirska Street on that evening. Later on, but for the time being, I should just like to say a few words about the testimony of the witnesses who charged him with being present in the house on that evening, though this has been explained in detail in my written brief. Let me mention first of all that today, after we have heard all evidence regarding Pionirska Street, it is the position of the Defence that the situation the way it was described by the witnesses and charged in the indictment simply could not have happened. The event in itself is not in dispute. This group of people was indeed locked up in the Omeragic house, as it is not in dispute that the room was set on fire. What is in dispute is what happened afterwards regardless of who the participants of the event were. Of the surviving witnesses, four were in the room and two had managed to escape earlier on. All of them claim that these men were next to the house, next to the rooms in question, and that it was right beneath the windows that they waited and stood guard to see if anyone should attempt to jump out of the window, and that they opened fire in such cases. They also claim that Mitar Vasiljevic was one of these individuals. However, Your Honours, not only would it have been quite impossible for these four persons, two women and two boys, to have jumped out of the window and found themselves in the vicinity of these armed men and avoid being killed by them, but also for the father of VG61 and another elderly gentleman to leave the house through the door. The man in question testified that he had passed by the house as he was going towards the creek. Since it is quite obvious that the fire was so severe that it was impossible to survive for any longer period of time inside the room, and that only those who managed to escape at the very beginning survived, we believe, Your Honours, that the people, the men who had set the house on fire, left the scene immediately and that, furthermore, they did not remain in the vicinity of the house, as it has been described by the witnesses. What makes me quite confident about this particular fact is the testimony of Witness VG87. He was able to follow the events from the attic. He was able to hear things and observe things. It was his wife who was with a group of people in his house at about 1100 that evening, who was taken in the direction of this house and never returned. She perished in the fire. Had there been any shooting from automatic rifles, as stated by the other witnesses, it would not have been possible for Witness VG87, whose house was some 50 or 80 metres away, not to have heard this or noticed this, and the only reasonable possibility is that this did not actually happen. I will not go into an analysis of the testimonies of the witnesses who claim to have seen Mitar Vasiljevic such as witnesses 78 and 101, who were sisters, and who either did not identify him or misidentified him in front of the Visegrad Hotel, so it is not credible that they saw him that night, or Witness VG13, who departed from her first statement made to the investigators in which she stated that she saw Mitar Vasiljevic using a flashlight, which is not credible because the person who is actually holding a flashlight is usually not visible. Witness VG13 then expanded on her statement, before the Court, saying that in the situations, she had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. described previously, involving Sredoje Lukic as a participant, and it is quite telling that until her cross-examination, she never once mentioned this name, although she mentioned it as many as 16 times in the statement she gave to the investigators. It is my submission, therefore, that because of the numerous contradictions and discrepancies, these witnesses should not be believed when they say that the event that took place in the evening happened in the way described, but I will not dwell on this any further because the Defence of Mitar Vasiljevic is a Defence of alibi. A lot of evidence has been provided to support this. There were witnesses who saw Mitar Vasiljevic riding a horse and falling off the horse in Visegrad that afternoon, and also witnesses who treated him in the medical centre, who took him to Uzice from Visegrad. In his closing statement, Mr. Groome stated that he did not believe Mitar Vasiljevic was injured in the way described or that he had ridden a horse at all that afternoon. Eye witnesses who saw this were referred to by him as friends and acquaintances of Mitar Vasiljevic. These were people who knew him but none of them had ever entered his home, so these were not special friends of his, especially not friends so close that they would risk perjury to state a fact such as this. Let me just remind you that in his testimony, Mr. Roy, an investigator of the Prosecution, in response to a question put to him by the Defence, confirmed that he had interviewed a person of Muslim ethnicity who confirmed that she was a witness to the fact that Mitar Vasiljevic had ridden a horse and fallen off the horse in the centre of Visegrad, but this person was never brought to testify before this Tribunal. What is much more important than the witness statements in the view of the Defence, is the medical documentation, which shows very clearly that Mitar Vasiljevic's alibi is well-founded. Apart from the eye witnesses who saw him fall off a horse, his alibi is also confirmed by people such as Dr. Loncarevic, who gave him first aid in the health centre in Visegrad, and then referred him to Uzice; people who accompanied him in the ambulance, the driver, Mr. Savic, and Mr. Novakovic, the financial manager of the health centre, who was in the vehicle. Then their stop in Vardiste and the testimony of Mitar Vasiljevic's uncle, who saw them there. What is very important is the fact that when the ambulance arrived in Uzice, according to the driver, this was before 9.00 p.m., which is the official time recorded as the time of his admission to hospital in Uzice, or rather the official time is 9.35 that evening. This must be the established time, although it is quite possible that the vehicle arrived earlier and that various formalities concerning his admission to hospital were being implemented so that the time gap can be explained by the time needed to fill in all the forms and to have the patient admitted to hospital. This is Exhibit P137, which is a hospital ledger -- the hospital admissions ledger, where persons brought in from the battle-front were recorded. This term was contested here and I think that we put in a lot of effort to establish why all the patients coming from a certain area, which was in Bosnia and Herzegovina, would be listed as having come from the battlefield, even if they arrived as patients with diseases that were not injuries suffered by soldiers. Examples were provided during the proceedings to show that all those who arrived from the territory affected by war in Bosnia and Herzegovina were entered into the books as persons coming from the war front. The Prosecution doubted the medical history, Exhibit P138, because it states that Mitar Vasiljevic was injured by falling on to a flat surface on the battle front. It has already been explained why the term "battlefield" was used. It is true that he was injured by falling on to a flat surface, because he fell in the middle of a street or a square, but what is not true is that he sustained the injury while falling either off or with a horse. We don't know why this was not entered. The witnesses who were examined here could only speculate about this, and they stated that this was either an omission or perhaps the manner in which the injury was sustained was not entered precisely because these were all people coming from a battlefield. We wished to bring Dr. Dr. Jovicevic here, who was the doctor who officially admitted Mitar Vasiljevic to hospital that evening because Dr. Moljevic was only a member of the screening team that evening, but Dr. Jovicevic was the doctor who was on duty, and in the concluding arguments of the Prosecution, it was pointed out that this witness was not brought to testify here. I have to say that I deeply regret that we were unable to bring this witness here, although it is doubtful whether he would remember why he hadn't noted down this fact after so much time has passed, but I wish to say that the reason he did not come was not only because he is suffering from back pain and because he has undergone an operation on his spine, but also he refused to come, saying that he did not recognise this Tribunal and that he was awaiting a law on cooperation between Yugoslavia and this Tribunal which would make it incumbent upon him to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I remonstrated with Mr. Groome about giving us material that is not in evidence. Please do not tell us what is not in evidence. If it's not in evidence, we do not consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Okay. [Interpretation] In my view, however, a sufficient number of witnesses have confirmed what is really important here. Some of them remembered Mitar Vasiljevic's case very well, especially because of the unusual injury he sustained, that is a fall off a horse, and apart from Mr. Moljevic, who was a patient in the orthopaedic ward, Dr. Jovanovic also remembered this, as did the nurse, Slavica Pavlovic, who brought with her a ledger kept by the nurses in their own hand, which has been produced as Exhibit D31. This exhibit also shows that on the evening of the 14th of June, the patient Mitar Vasiljevic was admitted to the orthopaedic ward. In my view, what is especially important with respect to this documentation is Exhibit P136, which is the ledger in which all the patients in all the wards of this hospital were entered in 1992, containing the first and last name, the number of the medical history, the date of admission, and the ward to which the patients were referred. An inspection of this ledger, which is authentic beyond any doubt, and the authenticity of which has not been brought into question, it can be seen that the number 10.014, which is the code for the medical history, was actually the code given to the patients admitted on that day because the numbers follow in sequence, according to the time when the patients are admitted in chronological order. Several examples of this nature have been provided. They are listed in the Defence submission, and all the -- this information can be compared to the information in the other books, P137 and in the case of patients referred from the Visegrad Health Centre, and I'm referring to absolutely all of them who were referred to Uzice, data was entered both in ledger P137 and in ledger 136. It would not have been possible for anyone, including Mitar Vasiljevic, to forge this sort of documentation in any way, or to tamper with it. Let me just remind you that the ledger from Visegrad, and that is Exhibit D26, has also not been challenged, although its authenticity was checked, apart from a single entry which was referred to in Mr. Groome's closing statement, and that is that on the 14th of June, the first patient entered was a patient bearing the name of Sredoje, while the last name was altered so that it now reads Gogic and not Bajic, while it may actually have been Lukic, as it appears. In his closing argument, the Prosecutor addressed the position of the Defence that from the age column of the ledger, one can clearly see that this could not have been Sredoje Lukic, and that an obvious mistake must have been corrected. However, Mr. Groome thought that such an addendum was entered later on, in hand. But from the evidence submitted to support this, we were able to see the photocopy of the relevant page and also that in the column which contains numbers, number of patients, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which is something that is always entered in any case, that the first six digits represent the day, the month and the year of birth, and that the person in question was born on the 5th of February, 1927. Therefore, it is evident that it must have been some other person and not Sredoje Lukic, although it would not be so surprising for such a patient to be examined as the first patient on that day, because we have another example, which has also been relied upon by the Prosecutor, and that is that on the 7th of June, 1992, Milan Lukic, with his year of birth accurately registered, was registered as one of the patients in the book of patients. It was alleged that this had been done as some kind of alibi in view of the event which took place on the 7th of June, 1992. However, it is quite clear from that entry that Milan Lukic was not referred anywhere else. He was only examined and if we look closely at the testimonies of VG14 and VG32, the testimony I'll go back to later on when discussing these particular events, it is clear that both witnesses had noticed, as early as at Bikovac, that Milan Lukic had some kind of bandage or Band-Aid on his hand and that he had obviously seen a doctor for that, which, quite contrary to the position of the Prosecutor, is even more supportive of the Defence case that the document in question is authentic, and that it was impossible for -- for example, Mitar Vasiljevic, to have been injured on the 27th or 28th of June, as it is attempted to interpret from testimonies of some witnesses, in particular VG81, because such an entry does not exist, nor was any such alteration possible; whereas, witness Loncarevic, Dr. Goran Loncarevic, who admitted Mitar Vasiljevic to hospital, was himself injured on the 24th of June and transferred to the Uzice hospital. So although he personally does not remember the date when he examined Mitar Vasiljevic, and states the date as being such only on the basis of this information, this could not have been on the 27th or the 28th of June, as VG81 was trying to establish. For quite specific reasons, because here was a witness who stated that it was during that period of time, from the 14th to the 25th of June, he had seen Mitar Vasiljevic in various situations, together or without Milan Lukic, which is quite impossible. So when taking into account other medical documentation which is on record in this case, namely the book of surgeries at the orthopaedic department, D32, some other medical documents, as well as the medical documentation from the psychiatric ward where Mitar Vasiljevic was subsequently transferred, and the assessment of all these testimonies, testimonies of the medical staff, physicians and nurses alike, who certainly would not, for Mitar Vasiljevic, whom some of them could remember, some could not, as a patient of the hospital, falsely testify about this fact or participate in the forgery of such documents, and we believe that it is fortunate that such medical documentation was properly kept during these times, and properly preserved. I have to say at this point that much to his regret, Mitar Vasiljevic has not kept any of his medical documents or x-rays that he had from these examinations, checkups and the treatment in general, which would have significantly facilitated the proceedings before this Court. The proceedings which have been further complicated with the expert analysis of the x-rays which doctor Moljevic brought on the 1st of November, 2000, with other medical documentation and which was later on analysed by experts. Due to time constraints and the fact that this has already been mentioned in the brief, I'm not going to address the issue of the expert analysis of these documents, and whether or not it is possible that this is an x-ray of Mitar Vasiljevic or an x-ray which can be compatible to Mitar Vasiljevic. But I shall restrict myself to saying that even if the x-ray in question was not Mitar Vasiljevic's x-ray, that is of his leg, and even if it was erroneously marked as such at the hospital, and inappropriately handed over together with the rest of the medical documentation, this doesn't mean that any of these written documents that I have discussed can in any way be challenged and brought into question. Dr. Moljevic himself, during his examination-in-chief, when asked whether such cases of erroneous markings and confusion of x-rays had already happened, stated that unfortunately such cases are always possible, even today, and that he himself had a similar case. We believe that there is a possibility that, especially in view of the times, that x-rays could have been confused or mistaken. Mitar Vasiljevic did not give this as an x-ray of his leg, nor could he know, nor can I know, whether the x-ray in question is indeed the real one, that is his x-ray. Let me remind you that from the beginning of the proceedings, Mitar Vasiljevic has not disputed medical examinations and medical expert analysis, and he was quite agreeable with this documentation being appropriately checked and verified. Therefore, both in case, if this is accepted as an x-ray which did not belong of his leg, nothing from the statements of witnesses, in particular the statements of the ten witnesses that I mentioned in this respect, nothing can prove that Mitar Vasiljevic was not in this hospital undergoing treatment from the 21 hours 35 minutes on the 14th of July, 1992, until the 28th of July, 1992. I'm not going to mention testimony given by other witnesses who paid him a visit. I should just like to remind you of the statement given by -- or rather the testimony given by Mr. Roy from which testimony we can conclude that a Muslim national was in the same hospital at the same time and he had given a statement about that fact in 1997, prior to the issuance of indictment against Mitar Vasiljevic before this Tribunal. I believe, Your Honours, that the evidence clearly indicates that Mitar Vasiljevic, in view of the information that you have and which is identical with the exhibits, was indeed injured, that he was admitted to the health centre in Visegrad on the 14th of June, 1992, from where he was transported to the Uzice hospital, where he stayed a certain amount of time. Allow me, Your Honours, one more sentence concerning this issue. The Prosecutor expressed in his final submissions his doubt that Mitar Vasiljevic -- his remark that Mitar Vasiljevic was entered as the third-before-last patient on this list of patients and that this casts a certain doubt as to the time of admission of the patient, which unfortunately was not entered as a piece of information, except in six or eight cases which were recorded by a nurse in Cyrillic alphabet and who was the only nurse who actually entered the exact time of admission. This was simply not done. This number of six to eight entries is quite Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. insignificant in view of the overall number of other cases. Let me also remind you that only three patients before Mitar Vasiljevic, Dragan Filipovic, was examined. Dragan Filipovic had been wounded and was transferred to the Uzice hospital before Mitar Vasiljevic, and according to P137, he was admitted to Uzice hospital at 15.45, which means that he must have left Visegrad sometime before 2.00 in the afternoon, and that later on that day, as the third patient after him, Mitar Vasiljevic was examined and admitted, which is quite probable. Furthermore, if one bears in mind the fact that it was a Sunday and a holiday, and that only urgent cases reported for examination. [In English] Your Honour, I don't know to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think if you go on until half past, it will divide the remaining time into half.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This documentation, which can be verified in many ways, and which was introduced either through cross-examination or examination-in-chief of witnesses, as well as the examples which we ourselves discovered, shows how credible these documents are, and to what extent the documents from Visegrad are compatible with the medical documentation in Uzice with respect to patients who arrived there from Visegrad. It is true that omissions were made, which also happened in other cases of a similar nature, as explained by witnesses. For example, not all the columns were filled in in the medical history, so that, for example, Mitar Vasiljevic's medical history, P138, contains spaces for the day and time of injury, which were not filled in, but as witnesses explained in most cases this was not done. This goes to show that there was no intention to falsify anything or forge anything because this could have been entered at a later date, and then it could have been established with more or less difficulty. Let me remind you that the medical history was subject to analysis by an expert witness from the Forensic Institute of Holland at the request of the Prosecution, and that the Defence insisted that this be admitted into evidence, because it shows that the medical history was filled in using three different typewriters, which according to the expert findings, were in use in 1992, but the same typewriters were used when filling in data coming from different wards. It is evident, for example, that the same typewriter, which was used to fill in the name of the doctor from the psychiatric ward who took over the treatment of the patient, the psychiatric diagnosis and the date of release from hospital, all this information was filled in using the same typewriter which was obviously the typewriter which existed in that ward. This is only one piece of evidence which goes to show that the documentation is authentic, but as I understood from the Prosecution closing brief, the Prosecution did not challenge the authenticity of any of the exhibits I have referred to. For all these reasons, I submit that the medical documentation and witnesses who are either eye witnesses or indirect witnesses to Vasiljevic's injury, treatment, people who visited him in hospital, all this shows that from the 14th of June, 1992, in the afternoon, from the time he was taken to the health centre in Visegrad, it was quite impossible for him to be seen taking part in any incident, either on his own or with others on the territory of Visegrad. If I focus on issues raised by the Prosecution, showing that Mitar Vasiljevic took part, allegedly took part in various incidents prior to this event which would support the veracity of the charges against him, according to what the Prosecutor said, this would refer to the testimony of Witness VG80, who allegedly on two occasions during June of that year saw from the window of her house in Visegrad Mitar Vasiljevic on one occasion accompanied by several other men, and bearing arms. However, with respect to this event, this witness did not give even an approximate indication of the date when she allegedly saw Mitar for a few seconds in front of a nearby garage. If this is true, it could have been during the period when he was a reservist Prelovo and would visit Visegrad in uniform and with weapons. It is not evident that he knew any of the persons he was seen with or that they were members of any paramilitary or other unit. As for the second event when she allegedly saw Mitar Vasiljevic leaving her house, she may have been mistaken because this would have been several days before she left Visegrad so it could have been the last day of June, because she left Visegrad in early July, and she could not have seen Mitar Vasiljevic at that time. Another characteristic of this witness's testimony is that when she made her earlier statement to the police, she mentioned more than 20 names of Serbs who, according to her, had perpetrated acts in Visegrad but on that occasion she never mentioned the name of Mitar Vasiljevic. What is much more important, however, is the testimony of VG81, on which the Prosecution mostly relies, attempting by means of this witness to prove that Mitar Vasiljevic engaged in illegal activities in the period leading up to the 14th of June, 1992, and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will resume again at ten to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Before I evaluate the statements and testimonies of several Prosecution witnesses, which the Prosecution also made special reference to, I would just like to correct my statement about witness VG80, because it might have been understood that I said she saw Mitar Vasiljevic from her house, or which would refer to a family house. This was in fact a block of flats. With respect to Witness VG115, on which the Prosecution relies to support three different events, which allegedly took place before the 14th of June, 1992, I would like to say the following. With respect to events after the 14th of June, this witness claims that up to the 25th of June, she saw Mitar Vasiljevic in different ways which, in the view of the Defence, discredits this witness, who is on especially bad terms with the Vasiljevic family. The first of the events mentioned in the closing arguments of the Prosecution is the alleged confiscation of the identity card of this witness by Mitar Vasiljevic, and this is connected by the Prosecution with similar actions committed by Milan Lukic. Let me remind you that the wife of the accused was examined as a witness with respect to this circumstance, and she, like the accused, denied ever having had an encounter of this nature with the witness, with VG81, in the vicinity of her house, and let me correct myself. I said 115 when I was referring to this witness. I am in fact speaking of Witness VG81. She claims that at the time of the withdrawal of the Uzice Corps, and she says this was on the 19th of May, in the vicinity of the house of Mitar Vasiljevic, she was stopped at the checkpoint that had been set up there, that it was manned by three armed soldiers, and that Mitar Vasiljevic was carrying weapons and was wearing a black waiter's uniform and that his wife was also present. It is hard to say why this witness should testify in this manner, but it is evident that at that time this was a checkpoint of the Uzice Corps, manned by the soldiers she mentions, and that no one had the right to take part, especially not in the manner described, wearing a waiter's uniform, standing at this military checkpoint manned by the army. The time when this took place, and the time of the presence of the Uzice Corps, do not support this incident and so it cannot be given any weight in these proceedings. The second example referred to in the Prosecution closing argument is of a very serious nature, the claim that on the 19th of June, 1992, he was in a car, together with Milan Lukic, and that on that day, he took part in catching Rasim Torohan and pushing him into the car, thus participating in spiriting away a person who was never seen thereafter. This was also mentioned as happening on the 9th of June, both in the closing arguments and in the brief, but it is obvious that this is an error made by the Prosecution, because the witness spoke of the 14th of June as the date when this happened, not only in the statement she made Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. previously when she said that this event took place four or five days before she left Kosovo Polje, that is before the murder of Stanko Pecikoza, and she used this as a reference point for calculating the date, but also in her testimony during her examination-in-chief. If one looks at the transcript carefully, the date which appears as the 9th of June is not linked to Rasim Torohan because she first explained that on the 14th of June, she saw the group from Koritnik and then, when asked by Mr. Groome on page 1224, "Later on this day, did you have occasion to see Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic?" [Interpretation] She replied "yes," and she went on to describe an event involving a red pass at, that is on the day that she saw the Koritnik group, that is on the 14th of June. However at one point in time, she said that he -- she saw Igbala Kurspahic at that moment and then she said, "No, I apologise. This took place on the 9th of June. I have to concentrate a little." It is therefore obvious that she described the event involving Torohan, as she did with everything else, as happening on the 14th of June and that something else happened on the 9th of June. In Exhibit D34 which is the stipulation between the Prosecution and the Defence concerning this particular witness, this statement is also included as not in dispute, that is when she stated that she had eye witnessed the event on the 14th of June. If we bear in mind the fact that she said this had taken place at sunset, around 6.00, and if we know that according to the information that we received, the sunset was after 8.00 on that day, it is obvious that on that day, if such an event involving Lukic and Milan Torohan indeed happened, is not an event in which Mitar Vasiljevic took part. Nor was he present there. All the more so because the way the witness calculated the date when she claimed persistently before the Chamber that it was on the 19th of June, that Stanko Pecikoza was killed and that in view of that, on the day when she learned, she and others, when they learned about his death, they fled and crossed the Drina. So all the events happening before this date, including the killing of Nurka Kos which he claimed had taken place two days before, and she also implicates Mitar Vasiljevic in this event, she also calculated this date with respect to the date of Stanko Pecikoza's death. From official written documents, we see that Pecikoza was killed on the 20th of June. And looking back on these days, this event could have also happened not on the 14th of June but on the 15th of June, including all other events which took place a day later. It is obvious that she made up the participation of Mitar Vasiljevic in this event and in subsequent events too. We can also assume that there was a confusion in respect of other event that she also fabricated when she said that on the 10th of June, that is the day before Kordan Bajram, Mitar Vasiljevic, as a front-seat passenger in a green Zastava or some other similar type of vehicle, passed through the area and said some abusive words about Bajram meat, thus offending Muslims. We have to note that she did not mention the incident in the statement given to the OTP, although she said that she saw Mitar Vasiljevic during the period of one month approximately. However, she never mentioned an incident of this kind. It is our position, Your Honour, then, in respect of a testimony of this kind, a testimony which can obviously be assessed as inaccurate in many of its respects, one should not trust the first part either, in respect of which we do not have any reliable evidence, all we have are discrepancies and contradictions in her statement. Let me remind you that this witness is the person who had organised illegal recording of the gathering in Kosovo Polje in February last year. The gathering I do not wish to address because it has been sufficiently discussed in my brief, and in the arguments made by the Prosecution, so bearing all this in mind, and in case VG30 was really referring to his voice, I cannot of course exclude the intention, because we are dealing here with a witness who was brought here and confronted with the fact that she had sold out information and video tapes, so we cannot rule out the possibility that the witness in question could have intentionally provided this information, which would have led this lady witness to produce this evidence and to make all these pieces fall. The witness stated that it was the first time after she had seen the witness on TV that she learned about him, that it was not on the 27th or 28th of June, which was obviously inaccurate because the videotape before the beginning of the trial was submitted for analysis to an institute here in the Netherlands, sometime at the beginning of August, so this must have been planned much earlier than what she said. I addressed her testimony at some length in my written brief. Let me just say a few words about several other witnesses which we believe to be very important in terms of credibility of their evidence. One of them is Witness 105, who was referred to by Mr. Groome on several occasions in a rather touching manner. Allegedly it is from her testimony that we can conclude that Mitar Vasiljevic patted a little girl trying to convince her that her father was alive in Sarajevo, although we know that his body was found in the Drina. This was mentioned before the Court several times and I have to say, on the outset, that it is not true that this witness stated that it was on the 13th of June that she had been transferred to the fire department. During the examination-in-chief, in response to a question whether it was on the third day of Bajram that she arrived in the fire department, she replied that she knew it was a Wednesday but that she, being illiterate didn't know exactly when Bajram was, but however that she was sure it was on Wednesday. However in cross-examination, in response to a question that I asked, when confronted her with her prior statement, when she said it was on the 17th of June, she replied that, yes, indeed, she had arrived in the fire department on the 17th of June. However, what is even more important than this date is her claim that this person, whom she described as having patted the little girl and whom she identified as being Mitar Vasiljevic, that is her claim that this person had a mustache, and she repeated that twice in response to one of my questions. She didn't say anything specific in respect of Mitar Vasiljevic. She only said that she had heard this from other persons, and although she mentioned him several times, she failed to recognise him in the photo array. She identified a person whom I think she said she thought was from Kragujeac, so in spite of the fact that she said she had seen him on TV and in papers, she failed to recognise him, which makes this evidence unacceptable and one can only conclude that the individual so described was by no means Mitar Vasiljevic, not only because of the date, which is subsequent to the 14th of June, but for other reasons that I have just described. All this demonstrates a rather strange intention of the witnesses to implicate Mitar Vasiljevic in something that he could not have been implicated in. I have to repeat that up until the confirmation of the indictment, there had been only a few witnesses who had allegedly spoken about his misdeeds. However, after his arrest and after the beginning of these proceedings, the majority of the witnesses were interviewed and gave statements regarding his alleged participation. In relation to that, we have to analyse the identification conducted by the Prosecution, the identification which took place after Mitar Vasiljevic's arrest. They used a photograph of Mitar Vasiljevic taken in the detention unit in Scheveningen, together with a group of other photographs, although the witnesses could have seen him a number of times on TV and elsewhere, including the specific photograph taken in the detention unit. This is by no means reliable evidence and it should not be taken into account. The same goes for the dock identification. When it comes to the two witnesses who provided relevant evidence about Pionirska Street and who were not from the Koritnik group, I should only briefly address their testimony. I don't deem their testimony to be credible and reliable at all. Two of such testimony being only partially credible and one of them being totally incredible. The testimony of VG77 is probably accurate in so far as it -- she states that she passed through Pionirska Street on that day, that she saw a group of people at the Memic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. house, and that she spent five or ten minutes talking to them. She went on, down the street, together with her husband and father-in-law, and she stated that it was on the junction of Pionirska Street and this other street that she saw Mitar Vasiljevic standing together with a group of soldiers. Why this portion of her evidence is absolutely inaccurate? First of all, she stated that she knew Mitar Vasiljevic only from sight, that she had only seen him a couple of times as a waiter. So obviously she didn't know him very well. She failed to recognise him in the photo album, despite this procedure which would have led her to recognise him relatively easily. She stated that the person whom she identified as Mitar Vasiljevic was standing with a soldier who had a yellow hat, a fact which was not mentioned by any other witness. If we bear in mind the fact that VG87 had a very good view of what was going on, because that was the only thing he was doing at the time, being at the attic -- on the attic of his house, he stated that at the time of the arrival of this group of people, Mitar Vasiljevic was in the vicinity of his house, so it is quite obvious that he could not have been further down the street at the spot that she described. And that she was mistaken when she identified the person standing with the soldier as being Mitar Vasiljevic. However, her testimony is very significant in the part where she says that on that day, she did not see Witness VG115 at all, and when she explains where this witness in fact resided in Pionirska Street. She was quite certain that she hadn't seen her on that day. This is important because Witness 115, who claims not only to have been an eyewitness to the events in Pionirska Street and who, as is explained in the brief, tells a story which is totally incredible because she says it was sometime in the evening at about 19 hours or after 19, that it was just before dark, that it was warm, and we know that it was raining, and that she saw a group of people whom she joined briefly, and that all the Lukics and Zoran Vasiljevic and others in addition to Mitar Vasiljevic, were there accompanying them. This statement of hers in relation to Pionirska Street is evidently a total fabrication and does not even remotely correspond with the actual events, but it is interesting that she mentions meeting Witness 87. She says that she had a brief encounter, that they exchanged glances and that she was on her own. This can only mean that she heard something like this and that she worked it into her story, not knowing that this witness was accompanied by his or her parents-in-law, and not knowing many other details which she got completely wrong. If we bear in mind that this witness claims to have been an eyewitness to the murder and the fire on Bikavac, which is theoretically possible but hardly likely, this description of the events in Pionirska Street cannot be trusted. She says that in all these other situations, she also saw Mitar Vasiljevic and others perpetrating these crimes. This refers primarily to the events she describes which are not contained in the indictment, and about which evidence was not collected by the Defence, where she says that on one evening, she -- and she describes her house quite differently, because Witness 77 says she lives at the end of Pionirska Street and not on the spot that this witness described, that Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic and another soldier arrived on the spot and that she watched them allegedly entering a house in the neighbourhood and searching it with flashlights starting on the third floor, going down to the second floor, and finally the first floor, where they found the Kurspahic couple and she says that she allegedly heard them shooting that couple and that on the following day, she saw their corpses through the open door of the house and that they remained there for five or six days. Bearing in mind that the people who had arrived from Koritnik and the witness who entered the house and came back and said that she had found these people who had been murdered, we have to note not only that they were not at the door but inside the house, the wife next to the cooker and the husband on the settee, but also that they had not been shot, rather their throats had been cut. It is quite clear that this witness also fabricated the participation of Mitar Vasiljevic in this event, and she referred to it as an event that took place in late June, in the summer. The other alleged events which according to her took place in July are events I will not comment upon because it is evident that she invented at least the participation of Mitar Vasiljevic even if the events actually took place and the other persons she described did take part in them. There is just one more witness I would like to mention, and that is VG61, who was a hearsay witness and who heard his father saying who the perpetrators of the events in Pionirska were, although he was affected by this because he lost part of his family in this crime, and he probably wishes to implicate not only Mitar Vasiljevic but some others as well, it is evident that he could not have obtained this information from his father because we saw in this Court a video recording in which this man only about 20 days after this tragedy recounts his recollection of it and says how he managed to get to the front door when the fire started and how he managed to flee. And he says that he was unable to recognise the participants and that they were young people. He did not implicate anyone, including Mitar Vasiljevic, and it is not possible that he would have done so at a later date. Let me just add that this witness's statement, that some ten days later or immediately after the event took place, he learned about it from witness VG13, who came to where he was in the police station, that this is inaccurate if we bear in mind that this witness went there in late July or early August of that year. In any case, I submit that the testimony of this witness is not only because of the alibi but for all these other reasons, not credible and should not be relied upon. There is one other witness who was suggested by the Prosecution and that is Witness VG117, but I have dealt extensively with this witness in my brief and explained in detail why this witness cannot be relied upon, so I will not dwell on it now. I simply ask that you take into account the arguments I have put forward in my brief. Before I go on to my conclusion, where I will analyse the events on the Drina and the crime at which Vasiljevic was present, as well as my final conclusion, I will just briefly address what the Prosecutor stated about the Defence witnesses and the guarantees required. Let me just say that the Defence asked for guarantees for all the witnesses coming from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of whether they asked for them or not. Most of them did not. Because we, as Defence counsel, wanted to avoid unpleasant situations so this does not have the significance that the Prosecution attaches to it, and I would like to try to rectify a few other matters. The Prosecution in their brief stated that the encounter with Koritnik was not the first encounter between him and Mitar Vasiljevic or rather that Vasiljevic had been convicted of singing a song previously. The village in question is called Klasnik and not Koritnik, and Article 119 is mentioned. This was an offence for which a sentence of over ten years in prison was prescribed and from the expert report of professor Djurdjic, it can be seen that this crime was prosecuted and that the prescribed sentence was up to three years in prison, while the other crime to which the Prosecution refers was far more serious, that is the type of crime for Alija Izetbegovic, for example, was prosecuted. As I stated a moment ago, I will not expound on the other parts of my brief, which refer to the psychiatric expert report, because I have explained this at great length in my final brief. I will now discuss the event on the river Drina with which Mitar Vasiljevic is charged, the Drina River incident. In the Defence brief, relating to this event, undisputed facts have been put forward, on page 19 of their brief. I have not heard anything about these facts being challenged so I will simply draw attention to those facts which I feel are contentious and those which I feel are important. I will not dwell on the offence that happened at Bikavac and the behaviour of Milan Lukic, because this does not concern the accused in any way. I will speak at greater length about Mr. Groome's doubts that -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or suspicion that Milan Lukic was entered as a patient at the health centre. I have already mentioned this in my introduction and I said that two witnesses confirmed that they saw bandages on Milan Lukic and that they assumed he had seen a doctor so I will not go into this any further. This can be seen on pages 242 and 424 of the transcript. When they arrived and entered the Vilina Vlas Hotel, both witnesses heard and saw a soldier wearing a camouflage uniform who was complaining to Lukic that that fool, referring to Susnjar, had released the prisoners. Then Lukic discussed this with Susnjar who justified his action by saying he had not had anything to give them to eat for two or three days, while Lukic was unsuccessfully looking for the keys to lock up the people who had been brought in, both witnesses noticed Mitar Vasiljevic leaning against the counter at the reception, at the entrance to the swimming pool area, and this is in disputable. What is disputable is that Witness VG32, who had seen Mitar well enough to see the insignia on his shirt pockets, to see that he was not armed, and that his arms were crossed. Had he had a rifle, or had a rifle been next to him, this witness would certainly have mentioned it, but it's evident that Mitar did not have a rifle and that counter to the testimony of -- and that the testimony of Witness VG14, which is different, is actually the true story, is incorrect, especially if we bear in mind that Mitar was holding a gun. In 1998, he said that he had seen Mitar carrying a semi-automatic rifle, and this was accepted by Ms. Korner as correct, because when the Defence put the question to him, the witness was unable to remember this, but he stated that he knew about weapons and that he was familiar with them. Both witnesses, to be sure, testified that they saw Mitar Vasiljevic on the stairs holding an automatic rifle. VG14 says that this was the rifle he had described previously and VG32 described it as a Kalashnikov. The Defence submits that the witnesses testified falsely on this occasion with the intention of implicating Mitar Vasiljevic as a co-perpetrator of the tragedy that had taken place because they assumed that he could have done something or they considered, without any proof, that he was part of Milan Lukic's group at the time when they made their first statements about this event. Although there are many discrepancies between the statements of these two witnesses, in important and less important details, let me mention only a few. According to one, when leaving Vilina Vlas, there were five persons in the Yugo car. According to the other witness, there were six, which is really difficult to believe. According to Witness VG32, they walked abreast toward the River Drina in a row so that he was unable to cross from one side to the other, and approach his relative, and Witness VG14, who says that they moved in single file, and that Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic were on their left, while he said in his statement to the investigators that they were on their right. It is much more important to note what they say about the moment when they were lined up facing the river, and when Witness VG32 says that Meho Dzafic first started to beg and then his brother-in-law, but that this was interrupted by the shots, and that he did not hear Mitar Vasiljevic utter a single word, either then or just before, while he was in -- close to him. Witness VG14, on the other hand, says that he heard only Meho's voice but that allegedly he heard Mitar reply to him and he obviously invented this because, had this really happened, VG32 would also have heard it. And he says that after these words were spoken, the shooting began. If we bear in mind that Meho was shot, that he was hit even before shots were heard, then certainly what Witness VG32 said is more credible, that Meho was hit and that no one, including Mitar, could have replied to his appeal. What is quite important to establish in this case is who actually shot at these people, because the two witnesses were not in a position to see that, which is accepted by the Prosecution. However, they make a conclusion that Mitar Vasiljevic took part in the incident by the mere fact that he was armed. And also by the testimony of VG32, who said that after the order was made to open fire, he heard -- he had heard three clicks of the weapon switching from automatic to single fire. And VG14 heard four shots, one of them was muffled, from the rifle with the silencer. Both witnesses, in particular VG32, made several statements about this event, first to the BH MUP and then in 1998 to the investigators of the OTP, and it was on the basis of these statements that the initial indictment was confirmed. However, neither of them at that time mentioned the fact that they mentioned before the Court. VG32 explained this by saying that when he initially gave the statement to Mr. Hansen in 2001 unlike the statement that he made in 1998 when the investigator did not allow him to expand, he wanted to provide more details. The investigator, however, told him that this was not important. This story is not credible because one knows very well that the investigators always ask for as many details as possible, and this is not an unimportant detail. This is a significant detail. Investigator Hansen asked him to try and think hard and try to remember what he heard at the Drina River. When he said that he had heard a click, Mr. Hansen asked him, "Sir, please, think hard now and tell me how many clicks you heard." The witness replied, "I rewound the tape. I was sure that I heard three clicks." Not only is this explanation by the witness illogical and unacceptable, that is that he was able in a few seconds to remember the details which had taken place nine years before, but also, it is strange that the witness later stated that this remained imprinted in his memory, although we know that he had not mentioned this in any of the previous statements. This was obviously a calculation on the part of the witness. His intention was to prove by this the direct participation of Mitar Vasiljevic in the event because he was aware that his statement that Mitar Vasiljevic was armed would not have been enough, so it was necessary for him to make this addition. It is the submission of the Defence that not only is it incredible and illogical that the witness should remember this nine years later, but also it is impossible to believe that the witness was able to hear that so clearly and that moreover he was able to hear three distinct clicks, not only because of the difficult situation he found himself in, but also because these three clicks, if they existed, happened probably at the same moment it was impossible to establish where they were coming from. Furthermore, we have to bear in mind the kind of situation these witnesses found themselves in. The same objection can be made in respect of witness VG14, whose testimony is different from the testimony of VG32. He couldn't remember the number of clicks. However, he too remembered nine years down the line, and this is something that he had not mentioned in any of his previous statements, that he had heard four shots, one of them being muffled, obviously implying the sniper rifle with the silencer belonging to Milan Lukic. From such statements, which were made subsequently, one can conclude that neither the clicking nor the opening of fire took place at the same time, but in sequence. As for the shooting itself, this is perhaps possible -- this is possible because one soldier could fire several such individual shots, one after the other. So three or four individual shots that the witness could have heard, perhaps, does not mean that those hits should have necessarily come from three or four different rifles, and that that should be the case here as well.
